packet.headline_seed: Canada flight cancelled after child refuses to wear seat belt
packet.description_seed: The incident has sparked a debate over child safety and discipline on commercial planes.

what: Canada flight cancelled after child refuses to wear seat belt

clean_source_blocks.text: The incident has sparked a debate over child safety and discipline on commercial planes.

The cancellation of a flight in Canada after a child refused to wear a seat belt has reignited a debate about the etiquette and safety procedures relating to children travelling on planes. The Porter Airlines flight, which was preparing to depart from Victoria to Toronto on 6 August had to return to the terminal as a "young child was standing in their seat and would not secure their seat belt", the airline said. The delay meant the flight could not depart before the runway closed after midnight so passengers had to be rebooked on a flight the following day. The incident has split opinion about how children should be treated in such situations and how airlines should respond. Regarding the child's behaviour, Porter Airlines said "attempts by the accompanying parent and crew to address this were unsuccessful".

"The aircraft could not takeoff in this unsafe condition, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark," it added. Child aviation safety expert Lia Tuso told the BBC the Porter crew were protecting the safety of the passengers on the flight with their decision to stop the flight, as well as the child. "Unrestrained children can become projectiles," Tuso said, similar to unrestrained items of luggage, which can fly into passengers in the event of turbulence, especially during takeoff and landing. The incident has led to a debate online over how tolerant airlines should be to travelling families, and how strictly parents should enforce airline rules.

The cancellation of a flight in Canada after a child refused to wear a seat belt has reignited a debate about the etiquette and safety procedures relating to children travelling on planes.

The Porter Airlines flight, which was preparing to depart from Victoria to Toronto on 6 August had to return to the terminal as a "young child was standing in their seat and would not secure their seat belt", the airline said.

The delay meant the flight could not depart before the runway closed after midnight so passengers had to be rebooked on a flight the following day.

The incident has split opinion about how children should be treated in such situations and how airlines should respond.

Regarding the child's behaviour, Porter Airlines said "attempts by the accompanying parent and crew to address this were unsuccessful".

"The aircraft could not takeoff in this unsafe condition, so the crew elected to return to the terminal and have the two passengers disembark," it added.

Child aviation safety expert Lia Tuso told the BBC the Porter crew were protecting the safety of the passengers on the flight with their decision to stop the flight, as well as the child.

"Unrestrained children can become projectiles," Tuso said, similar to unrestrained items of luggage, which can fly into passengers in the event of turbulence, especially during takeoff and landing.

The incident has led to a debate online over how tolerant airlines should be to travelling families, and how strictly parents should enforce airline rules.

Some have said it was an example of what happens when parents are too "gentle" on their children. The Fox News morning programme debated it, with co-host Charles Hurt saying he supported physical discipline.

"We've all been those parents," he said. "But this is beyond the pale."

Other people have pointed out that sometimes children are afraid of flying and are not trying to be disruptive.

One passenger on the Porter Airlines plane, Aryeh Kozuch, told CBC News the child had not been unruly but had seemed scared.

"They just kept hiding under their seat. If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath."

Many have questioned why the whole flight had to be disrupted for one child and said the family should have been removed.

This is what happened in 2018, when a father and daughter were filmed being ejected from a Southwest Airlines flight from Chicago to Atlanta.

TORONTO (AP) — A Porter Airlines flight in Canada was canceled last week after a young child refused to sit down and buckle up, forcing the plane back to the terminal and delaying it past the airport’s runway closure.

The Toronto-based airline said Sunday the parent and crew repeatedly tried unsuccessfully to secure the child in the seat before returning the plane to the terminal in Victoria International Airport in British Columbia to remove the parent and child.

Porter said removing the parent and child and their baggage delayed the Toronto-bound flight on Thursday past the airport’s 12:30 a.m. runway closure, forcing the remaining passengers to disembark.

Porter apologized to the other passengers, who were rebooked on a flight the following day.

VICTORIA, Canada (WKRC) — A flight in Canada had to be canceled last week after a young child stood on their seat and refused to put on their seat belt for takeoff, reports CBC Toronto.

The Porter Airlines flight was set to take off from Victoria International Airport in British Columbia to Toronto Thursday night, but it could not depart as a safety precaution due to the child, Brad Cicero, a spokesperson for the airline, said in a statement. The airplane had left the terminal and was on the runway, but despite efforts from the child's parent and cabin crew, the child would not sit down or allow their seat belt to be secured.

Flight attendants opted to return to the terminal and deplane all passengers because the time it would have taken to bridge the plane, deplane the child and parent, retrieve their baggage and refile paperwork would have caused the plane to depart too late. The runway at Victoria's airport closes at 12:30 a.m., and the flight was initially scheduled for an 11:03 p.m. departure.

"We apologize for the effect this had on other passengers, who were able to depart on a flight the following day," Cicero said in the statement.

Hillary Hertzberg’s first flight with Porter Airlines was anything but a smooth ride after a young child refused to sit down and wear a seatbelt, ultimately leading to the cancellation of the trip from Victoria, B.C. to Toronto.

She said some passengers ended up sleeping at the airport — and the next day at 1 p.m., they were back on the plane with the same passengers that had caused the delay.

Thursday night’s flight PD444 from Victoria International Airport to Pearson airport had to be rescheduled, Porter Airlines spokesperson Brad Cicero confirmed in an email Saturday evening.

The flight was set to take off at 10:30 p.m. Pacific time, according to the website FlightAware. Passengers were boarded shortly beforehand.

Hertzberg said Sunday that as flight attendants conducted their final safety checks, an announcement was made reminding passengers that everyone needed to comply with instructions.

Seated in row six, Hertzberg said she could see flight attendants repeatedly walking toward the back of the plane, near row 20, but initially did not know what was happening.
